name: Planck's Law
statement: A hot body's glow follows a fixed spectrum set only by its temperature.
statementAccent: a fixed spectrum set only by its temperature
meaning: Every object at a temperature radiates thermally, and Planck's law gives exactly how much it emits at each wavelength — the shape of the glow. The curve rises, peaks at a wavelength set by temperature, and falls, going to zero at short wavelengths rather than diverging, matching what is actually measured.
mechanism: The law follows from assuming that radiating oscillators can only emit or absorb energy in discrete packets proportional to frequency — quanta of size given by Planck's constant times frequency. This quantisation makes high-energy quanta exponentially unlikely, suppressing short-wavelength emission and curing the classical divergence. The assumption, incompatible with classical physics, is regarded as the birth of quantum theory.

examples.text: The afterglow of the Big Bang is the most perfect black-body spectrum known in nature, a Planck curve at about 2.7 kelvin — the sharpest confirmation of the law.
A heated filament, molten metal, or ember glows along a Planck curve set by its temperature, which is why colour tracks heat.
Stars radiate approximately as black bodies, so their peak wavelength and colour reveal surface temperature — Planck's law underlying the astronomer's temperature scale.

variants.name: The Rayleigh–Jeans law
variants.text: The classical long-wavelength limit of Planck's law, which agrees at long wavelengths but diverges to infinity at short ones — the 'ultraviolet catastrophe' that Planck's quantisation resolved.

variants.name: Stefan–Boltzmann and Wien
variants.text: The two summary laws that fall out of Planck's: integrating over all wavelengths gives the fourth-power Stefan–Boltzmann total, and locating the maximum gives Wien's peak wavelength.

whyItMatters: It is the founding law of quantum physics: to fit the measured spectrum of thermal radiation, Planck was forced to quantise energy, introducing the constant that bears his name and launching the quantum revolution. It also remains the exact description of thermal radiation, verified to extraordinary precision by the cosmic microwave background.

working.lead: Use it for the full spectrum
working.text: when you need emission at each wavelength, not just the total or the peak, Planck's law is the exact black-body curve.

working.lead: Recover the summary laws from it
working.text: integrate for total power (Stefan–Boltzmann) or differentiate for the peak (Wien) rather than treating them as separate facts.
apply emissivity and spectral features for real materials, which depart from the ideal black-body curve.

limits: The law describes an idealised perfect black body in thermal equilibrium. Real emitters have emissivity below one and material-dependent spectral features — emission and absorption lines, band structure — so they deviate from a pure Planck curve. Historically, Planck himself first regarded the energy quantisation as a mathematical device before its physical reality was accepted, extended by Einstein's 1905 work on the photoelectric effect. Within its idealisation it is exact and is the best-verified spectrum in physics.
misreadings: It is not a classical result patched up — the quantisation of energy it requires broke with classical physics and founded quantum theory. Nor does it describe real objects exactly; they emit less than an ideal black body and carry spectral features the smooth Planck curve omits.
origin: Derived by Max Planck in 1900, presented to the German Physical Society and revised with the quantum postulate that December. It resolved the ultraviolet catastrophe of the classical Rayleigh–Jeans law and introduced the quantum of action, launching quantum physics.
